fixes.explanation: Wisdom is a fine thing to ask for, but it's not what David asks for first. His first words are "Be merciful to me, O God…" (Psalm 56:1). The heading says the Philistines seized him in Gath, and mercy is what he opens with. I think when the walls are closing in, asking for the big thing first makes sense.
Not quite, friend. David says, "My enemies pursue me all day long, for many proudly assail me." (Psalm 56:2). Many, not a few. That's a whole crowd, and they pursue him all day long.

David does go to the wilderness in other places, like 1 Samuel 23:14, but not in this verse. Here he says, "When I am afraid, I put my trust in You." (Psalm 56:3). When the fear comes, he turns toward God. Keep your running shoes in the closet for this one.

Praise is something David does with God's word: "In God, whose word I praise…" (Psalm 56:4). The word for his enemies here is different. He says, "All day long they twist my words…" (Psalm 56:5). Twist is the one that fits the blank.
Trust is what David does with God: "…in God I trust." (Psalm 56:4). The blank is about his enemies, and David says, "All day long they twist my words…" (Psalm 56:5). Twist is the word that fits.
Cast down is right. David prays, "In Your anger, O God, cast down the nations." (Psalm 56:7). Notice who he's asking: he says it to God. Cast down is the request.
Lift up is the opposite direction, baker. David prays, "In Your anger, O God, cast down the nations." (Psalm 56:7). He's asking God to cast them down. Down, not up.
Laughing isn't in this verse, friend. David says, "Then my enemies will retreat on the day I cry for help." (Psalm 56:9). The word is retreat. On the day he cries for help, they pull back.

Thank offerings, yes. David says, "Your vows are upon me, O God; I will render thank offerings to You." (Psalm 56:12). He mentions the vows and the thank offerings side by side. That's a grateful man right there.
